rationale: B wins because its fourth angle, "Why Ramp is giving away an agent that finds six figures in savings," finds the sharper business-strategy puzzle sitting in the update. A is very strong, but "Ramp Turns Its $80 Billion Payments Network Into a Procurement Intelligence Engine" leans harder on an inferred moat than the facts can carry without an executive putting that on record. Both sets can be pitched after proof cleanup; B gives the founder the cleaner menu.
gaps_in_A: "Ramp Turns Its $80 Billion Payments Network Into a Procurement Intelligence Engine" overstates what the update proves; $80B purchase volume plus spend scanning does not yet prove a procurement-intelligence moat.
"the first public signal of Ramp explicitly turning payment data into procurement intelligence" is a dressed-up inference, not a supplied fact.
The data angle asks whether savings were identified or realized, but misses the median/distribution problem; an average $342,000 figure can be warped by a few large beta customers.
A misses the strongest pricing/business-model angle: the feature is included for existing customers at no extra cost despite allegedly finding six figures in savings.
gaps_in_B: "software nobody is using" overstates the facts; the update says savings came mostly from unused seats and auto-renewals, not that all the software was unused.
"quiet seat expansion" is not in the update. It may be true in SaaS generally, but it is imported color here.
"monetization deferred to a future enterprise tier" is a plausible read, but still an inference; the update says an enterprise tier is coming, not how Ramp will price it.
The journalist shape is a little softer than A's in places: "a business desk that runs corporate-waste stories" and "business-tech outlet" are usable, but less targeted than a real sub-beat.
